extracted.intended_audience: literate 18th-century readers; writers, critics, and gentlemen interested in taste, conduct, and composition
extracted.subtask_description: A set of short didactic essays giving principles for poetic composition, public taste, genteel behaviour, and remedies for absent-mindedness, illustrated with examples and classical parallels. Useful for writers, critics, and those cultivating a 'fine gentleman' demeanour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and majestic simplicity in popular verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Only Nature can have this Effect, and please those Tastes which are the most unprejudiced or the most refined; the Song's Sentiments are 'extremely natural and poetical, and full of majestick Simplicity which we admire in the greatest of the ancient Poets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-artifice or forced epigrammatic cleverness in ballads intended for broad appeal; favour simple, natural sentiments and a lofty simplicity like the ancients (illustrated by parallels to the Æneid and Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epigrammatical turns and points of wit for popular songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Had this old Song been filled with Epigrammatical Turns and Points of Wit it might perhaps have pleased the wrong Taste of some Readers; but it would never have become the Delight of the common People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing for wide public affection, do not substitute clever repartee or epigram for natural, affecting material—such tricks may please a limited 'wrong' taste but will alienate common readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sonorous language and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several Parts in it where not only the Thought but the Language is majestick, and the Numbers [sonorous;] ... the Language is often very sounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for sonorous rhythms and powerful, resonant phrasing in descriptive and heroic passages to achieve a 'majestic' poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated/dressy diction can enhance majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: At least, the Apparel is much more gorgeous than many of the Poets made use of in Queen Elizabeth's Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate 'gorgeous' diction or elevated 'apparel' of language may be preferable to mean or overly plain phrasing when the subject demands grandeur; match diction to subject-matter and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue technique with individualized details
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Catalogue of the Slain the Author has followed the Example of the greatest ancient Poets, not only in giving a long List of the Dead, but by diversifying it with little Characters of particular Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When listing many persons or items (e.g., battle-rolls), break monotony by inserting short, characteristic particulars about individuals to maintain interest and pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid familiar or commonplace names that destroy majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar Sound in these Names destroys the Majesty of the Description; for this Reason I do not mention this Part of the Poem but to shew the natural Cast of Thought which appears in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of using overly familiar, colloquial, or undignified names/terms in epic or majestic passages; such particulars can undermine the grandeur you intend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural, moving circumstances to produce pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be more natural or more moving than the Circumstances in which he describes the Behaviour of those Women who had lost their Husbands on this fatal Day?... The Thoughts of this Poem, which naturally arise from the Subject, are always simple, and sometimes exquisitely noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground emotional passages in believable, concrete, and natural details (widows washing wounds, kissing the dead) rather than contrived ornament, to move the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support critical judgments by citing classical parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall quote several Passages of it, in which the Thought is altogether the same with what we meet in several Passages of the Æneid... I should not have made use of [Latin quotations], but that I feared my own Judgment would have looked too singular... had not I supported it by the Practice and Authority of Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting high praise or a stylistic kinship to revered models, buttress your claim with specific classical parallels and quotations to persuade skeptical readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: A gentleman must conform to prevailing maxims of reason and good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: No Man ought to have the Esteem of the rest of the World, for any Actions which are disagreeable to those Maxims which prevail, as the Standards of Behaviour, in the Country wherein he lives. What is opposite to the eternal Rules of Reason and good Sense, must be excluded from any Place in the Carriage of a Well-bred Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genteel behaviour is not merely outward ornament—follow enduring rules of reason and good sense in conduct to deserve respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity and avoidance of reproach in speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity obliges a Gentleman to give no Part of Humankind Reproach, for what they, whom they Reproach, may possibly have in Common with the most Virtuous and Worthy amongst us. When a Gentleman speaks Coarsly, he has dressed himself Clean to no purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid coarse, reproachful language and public degradation of others; moral worth and humane speech matter more than fashionable dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unaffected negligence and ease as marks of true gentility
rubrics_metrics.description: By a thorough Contempt of little Excellencies, he is perfectly Master of them. This Temper of Mind leaves him under no Necessity of Studying his Air, and he has this peculiar Distinction, that his Negligence is unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine indifference to petty affectations—real ease and unconcern (not simulated negligence) signal true refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner virtue produces graceful demeanour
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm and unshaken Expectation of another Life, makes him become this; Humanity and Good-nature, fortified by the Sense of Virtue... The Change of Persons or Things around him do not at all alter his Situation, but he looks disinterested in the Occurrences with which others are distracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on moral and intellectual character—generosity, courage, and a steady mind—since internal virtues manifest as external grace and consistent behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: To be a Fine Gentleman is to be generous and brave
rubrics_metrics.description: In a word, to be a Fine Gentleman, is to be a Generous and a Brave Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize bravery and generosity as the core virtues; manners and appearance follow from substantive moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of absentness (thinking vs. vacant)
rubrics_metrics.description: I distinguish a Man who is Absent, because he thinks of something else, from one who is Absent, because he thinks of nothing at all: The latter is too innocent a Creature to be taken notice of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing distracted behaviour (in oneself or characters), differentiate productive immersion (thinking of other matters) from vacuity; the causes and remedies differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common causes of distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Either their Minds are wholly fixed on some particular Science... or are wholly taken up with some Violent Passion, such as Anger, Fear, or Love... or, lastly, these Distractions proceed from a certain Vivacity and Fickleness in a Man's Temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute absent-mindedness to plausible causes (intense study, passion, or vivacity) rather than mere stupidity; this informs judgment and how to address it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for being absent: learn from everything and participate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method I took to conquer it was a firm Resolution to learn something from whatever I was obliged to see or hear... I always make one of the Company I am in; though I say little myself, my Attention to others, and those Nods of Approbation which I never bestow unmerited, sufficiently shew that I am among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To cure distractibility, resolve to extract something from every experience and adopt an attitude of active participation (attentive listening, small signals of engagement) rather than mere passivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour/manipulation by a sovereign as humane discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: He punished his Courtiers for their Insolence and Folly, not by any Act of Publick Disfavour, but by humorously practising upon their Imaginations... He would, by a skilful Cast of his Eye and half a Smile, make two Fellows who hated, embrace... He would find an Opportunity to take some favourable Notice of him, and render him insupportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A playful, private use of wit and social manipulation can regulate court behaviour and punish folly without public disgrace—use imagination and small acts to alter reputations and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose recipients of favour by steadiness of temper
rubrics_metrics.description: He gave Fortune to none but those whom he knew could receive it without Transport: He made a noble and generous Use of his Observations; and did not regard his Ministers as they were agreeable to himself, but as they were useful to his Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When bestowing favors or power, prefer those who show temperate, steady character and usefulness to the larger public interest rather than those who will be undone by excess or flattery.
